title: the words, line by line, from Luke
hook: the words, line by line, from Luke

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rosary beads: five decades, a counting string. Your line was: hands busy, heart free. Today, the words on those ten beads. Day eleven.

It's the prayer people say fastest. At a wake, a room full of voices running it together so it sounds like one long word. A kid in Catholic school rattling it off in eight seconds. In football, a quarterback throws the ball deep with no hope left, and that pass still gets called a Hail Mary. Most people who know the words have never stopped to hear them. Where they came from. Who said them first. It turns out most of the prayer isn't new at all. It's lifted, line by line, from the first chapter of Luke's Gospel. Today, slowly.
screen: `SAID FASTER THAN ANY PRAYER.` → `A HAIL MARY PASS.` → `LIFTED FROM LUKE.`

segments.voice: The first line belongs to an angel. Remember day six, Gabriel in the room in Nazareth. In the Douay-Rheims Bible, his first words are: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Hail is just an old hello. Full of grace is your first word, on day one: a gift given, filled to the brim. The next line belongs to a relative. A little later in Luke, Mary goes to visit her cousin Elizabeth, who's also pregnant, and Elizabeth cries out: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Over the centuries Christians put those two greetings side by side, an angel's and a cousin's, and added two names: Mary, right after the angel's hail, and Jesus at the end. That's the whole first half. Every word of it, apart from those two names, is from Luke. Then the prayer turns. The second half isn't scripture. It's the Church speaking, and it was added later; the full form was settled in the sixteenth century. It goes: Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen. Listen to the shape. The first half says hello. The second half asks for something. And what it asks is small and huge at once: pray for us. Now, and at the very end. Catholics aren't asking Mary to do what only God does. They're asking her to pray with them, the way you'd ask a mother to. That's why it's said ten times on each decade. A greeting, then a request, again and again, like a heartbeat, while the mind thinks about Jesus. Say it fast and it's a blur. Say it slowly and you're standing in two rooms in Luke's Gospel.
screen: `AN ANGEL'S HELLO.` · `A COUSIN'S BLESSING.` · `THEN THE CHURCH ASKS.` · `PRAY FOR US, NOW AND AT THE END.` · then, large: `A GREETING, THEN A REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A forty-five-second sit. Let your breath slow down. On the breath in, think of a greeting: hello to someone you love. On the breath out, think of a request: one thing you need right now. In, a greeting. Out, a request. If you pray the Hail Mary, you can say it once, as slowly as you've ever said it. The bell holds the time.
The rosary, the Hail Mary. An angel's hello and a cousin's blessing from Luke, then the Church's request: pray for us. Eleventh word.
screen: `THE ROSARY, THE HAIL MARY — your 11th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a greeting, then a request. Today, before you ask anyone for anything, greet them first, properly. Day eleven.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MOST MISUNDERSTOOD ROOM IN THE BUILDING.`

howItsDone: Catholics say the Hail Mary ten times on each decade of the rosary, and on its own at many moments of the day; its first half comes from Luke 1:28 and 1:42.

fork.setup: Mary, newly pregnant, walks into her cousin Elizabeth's house. what does Elizabeth say?
fork.reveal: "blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." her words became the second line of the Hail Mary.

original.note: Latin: hail Mary, full of grace. the opening of the prayer as it was said for centuries.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fast prayer, or a desperate football pass.
what it means: an angel's greeting and a cousin's blessing from Luke, then a request: pray for us.
what a scholar hears: Luke 1:28 and 1:42 joined in Western devotion by the Middle Ages; the petition settled in the 1568 Roman Breviary; kecharitomene, the Greek behind full of grace.

notes: Luke 1:28 and 1:42 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording and punctuation.
The second half's standard form: generally dated to the 1568 Roman Breviary of Pius V; the voice says 'settled in the sixteenth century'. Confirm.
The traditional English Hail Mary is quoted in the voice without quotation marks; confirm it is fine to present it as a traditional public-domain text.
Hail Mary pass: popularized by Roger Staubach in 1975; confirm.

Voice now says two names were added to Luke's words (Mary and Jesus); the earlier draft said one name, then referred to 'those two names'. Pairing the two greetings is older in Eastern liturgies, so the scholar line now says 'joined in Western devotion by the Middle Ages'. Confirm dating.
